appraisal_events.evidence: The desired crémière, once present, is « réduite à elle-même », her nose « plus rond que je ne l’avais cru, qui donnait une idée de bêtise » ; then the Figaro announcement of Mlle Léa at the Trocadéro: « Ce fut comme si on avait brutalement arraché de mon cœur le pansement sous lequel il avait commencé, depuis mon retour de Balbec, à se cicatriser. Le flux de mes angoisses s’échappa à torrents. »
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator's morning of contemplative mastery collapses twice over: his erotic projection onto the dairy girl deflates into « le réel immobile » and the pretext of the letter exposes him as timid and scheming, and then the printed name of Léa reopens his jealousy in full flood. The passage plainly endorses this as loss of composure and of emotional ground, not as attained intimacy.

appraisal_events.evidence: The narrator sets out Albertine's four successive stages of lying — « Oh non, ce n’est pas du tout une femme comme ça, c’est une femme très bien » ; « Je ne la connais pas » ; « Mais voyons, naturellement, c’est connu comme tout ! » ; « Elle a eu le béguin pour moi » — and concludes that « tout ce qu’elle avait raconté dès le début n’était qu’un tissu de contes mensongers ».
appraisal_events.explanation: Albertine is systematically discredited: her speech is anatomized as a reproducible mechanism of contradiction and forgetting, and she is denied even the dignity of a single confessed lie, since she would rather retract one statement than admit the whole tissue. The narrator presents this taxonomy as established knowledge, not as a suspicion.

status_effects.explanation: He ends the passage stripped of the calm of the contemplator and of the illusion sustaining his desire, with his anxieties returning « à torrents » at Léa's name; he loses, rather than gains, leverage over his own feeling.
Her local standing falls sharply because the passage exhibits her habitual mendacity as a fixed four-stage pattern culminating in the phrase « un tissu de contes mensongers ».

Although discredited, she gains local hold over the narrator: her absence and the mere possibility of her connection with Léa are enough to dictate his state of mind and reopen the wound that had begun to heal.

ambiguities: The crémière episode briefly rises toward erotic exaltation (« je sentis que leur tourbillon m’emportait, le cœur battant, dans la lumière et les rafales d’un ouragan de beauté »), but it is framed on both sides by disenchantment and then cut off by the Figaro; the passage stages arrested desire rather than realized intimacy, so it is read as part of the negative movement rather than as a countervailing positive one.

The discredit of Albertine is generalized from past instances and is explicitly not established for Léa (« pour cette dernière je n’en étais qu’à la première affirmation et j’ignorais si Albertine la connaissait »), and the narrator concedes the truth « était peut-être moins grave que je n’étais porté à le croire »; the diminishment is nonetheless read as narrator-endorsed because the lying pattern itself is presented as verified fact.
